claims.text: The initial system is a zirconium-alloy fuel-cladding substrate with an elemental Cr coating deposited by physical vapor deposition.
Reactive magnetron sputtering in Ar–N2 at a substrate temperature of approximately 400–500 °C will form a Cr2N interlayer at the Cr/Zr interface.
The sputtering intervention will produce a thin, continuous Cr2N interlayer.
The interfacial Cr2N layer will act as a diffusion barrier.
Formation of Cr2N reduces atomic mobility at the Cr/Zr interface.
Reduced interfacial atomic mobility limits Cr–Zr interdiffusion during high-temperature steam exposure.
An unmodified elemental Cr coating is susceptible to Cr–Zr interdiffusion and premature failure during high-temperature steam exposure.
The Cr2N-modified coating will exhibit less Cr–Zr interdiffusion than the unmodified Cr-coated baseline after steam exposure at approximately 1200 °C for up to 2 hours.
The Cr2N-modified coating will undergo delayed degradation relative to the unmodified Cr-coated baseline in high-temperature steam.
The Cr2N interlayer will extend coating lifetime relative to an unmodified elemental Cr coating.
The Cr2N-modified coating will maintain corrosion resistance under subcritical-water conditions at approximately 350 °C.
The Cr2N barrier will not adversely affect coating performance under normal operating conditions.
Steam exposure at approximately 1200 °C for up to 2 hours represents the stated accident-relevant performance boundary.
Subcritical-water exposure at approximately 350 °C represents the stated normal-operation performance boundary.
Cr2N brittleness or adhesion problems during repeated thermal cycling could compromise long-term coating integrity.

The hypothesis is falsified if Cr2N-modified samples show interdiffusion, mechanical degradation, cracking, delamination, or coating failure statistically equivalent to or worse than the unmodified controls under matched conditions.
